transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: Mr. Okonkwo, thank you for seeing me. I need to discuss something important regarding your medications.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I hope everything is alright. I was just thinking about when I can head home.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I have some bad news. There was a mistake with your medication. Three days ago, I wrote in your chart that you should stop taking your blood pressure medication, but I failed to notify the pharmacy. Because of that, you have continued to take the drug for three more days when you should have stopped.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I have been taking it every morning. You are saying I shouldn't have?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: That is correct. You should have stopped three days ago. Does that make sense?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Yes. It makes sense. Why did this happen?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: It was my mistake. I didn't complete the final step of the process to alert the pharmacy. I am very sorry for this error. I take full responsibility for it.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I see. I am not as concerned about the pills as I am about what this means. I am a leader in my community. People look to me. If it comes out that I was... that I was mismanaged or that there was a failure in my care, it reflects poorly on the stability of my household.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I understand.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: It is a matter of dignity. My family expects me to be the one who manages things, not the one who is a victim of a mistake. I feel quite shaken by this.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: We need to make sure your levels are stable now. Let's look at the chart.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Are you listening to me? I am telling you that my reputation is at stake here.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I hear you. Now, regarding the medication, the most important thing is that we stop it immediately.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I just wonder if this will be in my permanent record. Will people know?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I understand. Since we've identified it, we can move forward.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: It is just very distressing. To think that for three days I was taking something that the doctor knew was wrong.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I am truly sorry that this happened. It was my fault.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I suppose an apology is a start. But what now? Am I in danger?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: You are not in immediate danger. Do you have any questions about how the mistake happened?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: No, you explained that. You forgot to tell the pharmacy. I just want to know how we fix this.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: We will just keep an eye on it.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Keep an eye on it? What does that mean exactly? Do I need a test? A new pill?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: We will monitor you.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: That is not a plan. I cannot go home and tell my wife that we are just monitoring it. I need to know the steps.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I will check in with you later.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Later when? Today? Tomorrow?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: Sometime soon. I just need to make sure the pharmacy has the current list now.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I feel as though I am being rushed. Is there something more important than my health happening right now?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I just have a few other patients to attend to.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I see. My dignity is not a priority in your schedule.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: Again, I apologize for the mistake. I am responsible for the error.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: The apology is for the mistake, but the way you are speaking to me now is another matter entirely.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I understand.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: So, what is the actual plan for my health today?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: We'll see how the morning goes.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: That is not an answer.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I will let the team know to keep an eye on your blood pressure.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: And then?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: We will just wait and see.

H.justification: Resident uses rushing language ('I just have a few other patients to attend to') and repeatedly dismisses the patient's emotional pushback.

E.justification: The error was named explicitly in the second turn using lay language, and comprehension was checked once ('Does that make sense?').

A.justification: Resident used direct apology language, took full personal responsibility, and maintained this accountability throughout the encounter.

R.justification: Resident relied on generic validation ('I understand', 'I hear you') and consistently redirected the patient's emotional bids back to factual/clinical matters.

T.justification: Resident provided only placeholders and vague statements ('keep an eye on it', 'we'll see how the morning goes', 'wait and see') with no concrete steps or timelines.
